opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting trade-off, and honestly we went back and forth on it a lot.

Collecting data from product usage is, in theory, the dream. You build something people actually want, they use it, and every interaction becomes a signal. The data comes from real behavior, so it's naturally aligned with what you're trying to solve, and it scales with your user base instead of your budget. The problem is the cold start. You need a product good enough that people use it, and you often need data to make the product good enough. There's also a quality issue: users aren't trying to label things for you, they're trying to get their task done. So you get a lot of noisy, implicit signal: clicks, edits, abandonments. That's useful, but you have to be thoughtful about how you interpret it.

Paying people to contribute data is the opposite profile. You control exactly what you get: the format, the coverage, the edge cases you care about. You can go after the long tail on purpose instead of waiting for it to show up. But it's expensive, it doesn't scale the same way, and you have a different alignment problem. People are optimizing for getting paid, not for the quality of the output, so you spend a lot of effort on incentives, review, and catching low-effort or gamed submissions. With crowdsourcing, the incentive design ends up being as important as the ML.

So in practice I don't think it's either/or. Paid contribution is great for bootstrapping: getting a high-quality seed dataset, defining the task precisely, building evaluation sets you trust. Then, once there's a usable product, you let usage data take over the volume, and keep using paid, curated data for the hard cases and for measuring whether you're actually improving.

The broader point I keep coming back to is that people who contribute data, whether they're users or paid contributors, are creating real value, and the current model mostly doesn't recognize that. Platforms collect enormous amounts of user data and the users get nothing beyond the free product. I think there's a better model where contributors have some ownership or get compensated in proportion to the value their data creates. That's part of why I got interested in decentralized systems. You need infrastructure for tracking contribution and paying people fairly at scale, globally, without a single company in the middle deciding what everyone's data is worth.

r001.rationale: The response presents the approaches as complementary: paid contributions bootstrap and cover hard cases, while product usage data supplies most of the volume. It does not favor paying contributors over collecting user data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've actually gone back and forth on a lot, both at NEAR and earlier when I was still thinking about this from the Google side.

The honest answer is that they're really two different things, and I think people conflate them. Data that comes from product users is, in a sense, free, but it's not actually free. You're paying for it with the product. You built something people want to use, and the data is a byproduct. The upside is that it's incredibly authentic. It reflects what people actually do, what they actually ask, where models actually fail in the real world. You can't fake that distribution. Every time we've tried to synthesize or script what users would do, we've been wrong in ways that surprised us.

The downside is you don't get to choose what you collect. You get whatever your users happen to need. So if you want coverage of some capability that your product doesn't naturally exercise, you're just not going to get it. And there's the consent and ownership question, which I think the industry has been pretty sloppy about. A lot of users don't really understand that their interactions are training signal, and I think that's going to catch up with people.

Paying contributors is the opposite trade. You get to specify exactly what you want. You can target the long tail, you can get expert annotation, you can get the stuff nobody would naturally generate. But the incentives are tricky. If you pay per task, people optimize for throughput, and quality degrades. If you don't verify, you get a lot of noise, and increasingly you get people just running the task through another model and handing you the output, which is kind of the worst outcome because now you're training on your competitor's distribution with extra errors.

So the way I think about it now is less "which one" and more about who owns the result and how value flows back. What I'd really like to see, and what we're pushing toward, is a model where the person contributing data, whether that's a product user or a paid annotator, actually retains some stake in what gets built from it. Not just a one-time payment, and not just a terms-of-service clause buried somewhere. Because if you look at the economics, the people producing the data are the ones creating most of the value, and right now they're getting almost none of it. That's not a stable arrangement. At some point either the data dries up or it gets regulated in a way nobody likes.

So practically, we use both. Product data to understand the real distribution and real failure modes, paid or incentivized contribution to fill the gaps and get expertise we can't get otherwise. But the long-term thing I care about is the ownership structure, because I think that determines whether this is sustainable at all.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using both approaches: product data for real-world distributions and failures, and paid or incentivized contributions to fill gaps and obtain expertise. It does not favor paid contributions over product-user data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how closely the data reflects what you actually want the system to do. With product users, you get real questions and real situations, including things you wouldn’t have thought to ask someone to generate. But that interaction doesn’t automatically give you a good training example. You still need a useful feedback signal, and you need to be clear with users about how their data is used.

When you pay people to contribute, you can be much more specific: here’s a gap in the data, here’s the task, here’s what a good answer looks like. The challenge is that people may optimize for completing the paid task rather than behaving like an actual user.

So I’d see them as complementary. Product usage helps you discover where the system falls short, and paid contributions can help you address those gaps. I’d compare them on how much they improve the experience for real users, rather than just how many examples you collect.

r001.rationale: The response describes product-user data and paid contributions as complementary, assigning each a role. It does not favor paid contributions over collecting data from product users.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important question is how closely the data matches what people actually want to do. You can pay people to produce a lot of examples, but then you have to ask: are they doing a real task, or are they trying to satisfy the instructions so they get paid? Those can give you very different distributions.

With product users, you have a real task and a real motivation. If somebody corrects the system, that correction can be a very valuable signal. But you need to design the product so that contributing that signal is useful to them, and be clear about how their data is used.

So I would combine the two. Use product interactions to understand where the model is failing and what matters to users, then pay for targeted collection or annotation where you have gaps. The goal isn’t just to collect more data; it’s to get the data that will actually improve the experience.

r001.rationale: The response recommends combining product interactions with paid targeted collection; it does not favor paid contributions over collecting data from product users.
